subChunks.title: Setup for Vite + React
subChunks.hookHtml: Ninety percent of new React projects today use Vite. Tailwind v4 made setup dramatically simpler: two commands, one CSS import, no config file. Understanding the setup sequence — and the one scanning rule that can still catch you out — is a genuine job-readiness skill.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Installing Tailwind v4 in a Vite + React project

Two commands. No config file. No PostCSS setup required.

# 1. Create the project (if you haven't already)
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts
cd my-app

# 2. Install Tailwind and its Vite plugin
npm install -D tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite

Configure the Vite plugin

Open vite.config.ts and register the Tailwind plugin:

import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    tailwindcss(),  // ← this is the entire Tailwind setup
  ],
})

Import Tailwind in your CSS

Replace all contents of src/index.css with a single line:

@import "tailwindcss";

That single import replaces the three @tailwind base/components/utilities directives from v3. Import the file in src/main.tsx:

import './index.css';

Automatic content detection

Tailwind v4 scans your project files automatically — no content array to configure or maintain. For the vast majority of Vite + React projects you are fully set up at this point.

The dynamic class trap — still applies in v4

Automatic detection changed how file paths are found. It did not change how class names are found. Tailwind v4 is still a text scanner — every class string must appear verbatim in a scanned file.

// BROKEN — 'bg-blue-500' never appears as a complete string in source
const cls = `bg-${colour}-500`;

// CORRECT — full strings are visible in source
const colourMap = {
  blue:  'bg-blue-500',
  red:   'bg-red-500',
  green: 'bg-green-500',
};
const cls = colourMap[colour];

Safelisting classes from external data

When class names come from a CMS, database, or API, use @source inline() in your CSS:

/* Safelist explicit class names */
@source inline("bg-red-500 bg-green-500 text-red-800 text-green-800");

/* Pattern syntax for a whole family */
@source inline("{bg,text}-{red,green,blue}-{100,500,900}");

Cordell: "Automatic detection changed which files are scanned. It did not change how class names are found. The scanner reads plain text — if a complete class string does not appear verbatim in a scanned file, that class does not exist in production."

storyBeats.speaker: Maester Cordell
storyBeats.text: Tailwind v4 changed all of that. Two commands and one CSS import — that is the entire setup. Add the Tailwind plugin to vite.config.ts, put a single line in your CSS file: @import 'tailwindcss'. No config file. No PostCSS. Done.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Style this configuration panel from scratch — remember the class names without looking them up. A light slate background, visible border, rounded corners, and comfortable padding on the panel. Large, semi-bold, dark slate text for the title. Small, green, medium-weight text with a top margin for the status.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the complete setup sequence for Tailwind v4 in a brand-new Vite + React TypeScript project, from the first npm command to verifying styles are working. Explain what @tailwindcss/vite does, what @import 'tailwindcss' replaces, and what the one production trap is that still exists despite automatic content detection.

questions.prompt: What is the single CSS declaration needed to activate all of Tailwind v4 in your stylesheet?
questions.explanation: Tailwind v4 replaces the three @tailwind directives from v3 with a single standard CSS @import. This one line activates the base reset, all utility classes, and the theme system.

questions.prompt: A developer writes `const cls = \`bg-${colour}-500\`` where colour comes from a prop. The class never applies in production despite Tailwind v4's automatic detection. Why?
options: Tailwind still scans as plain text — complete class strings must appear verbatim; 'bg-blue-500' is never a complete string in source
Automatic detection does not scan component props or variables
Template literals require a @source inline() entry to be detected
v4's Vite plugin only scans .tsx files, not dynamic expressions
questions.answer: Tailwind still scans as plain text — complete class strings must appear verbatim; 'bg-blue-500' is never a complete string in source
questions.explanation: Automatic detection changed which files are scanned, not how class names are found. The scanner still performs text matching — 'bg-blue-500' must appear as a complete string somewhere. A template literal like `bg-${colour}-500` produces only the fragments 'bg-' and '-500'. The fix is a lookup object: const map = { blue: 'bg-blue-500', red: 'bg-red-500' }.

questions.prompt: A team is upgrading from Tailwind v3 to v4. They have a tailwind.config.js, a postcss.config.js, and three @tailwind directives in their CSS. What is the correct migration sequence?
options: Install @tailwindcss/vite, add it to vite.config.ts, replace the three @tailwind directives with @import 'tailwindcss', move theme customisations to @theme {} in CSS, delete tailwind.config.js and postcss.config.js
Just upgrade the tailwindcss package to v4 — it is backward compatible with v3 configuration files
Delete tailwind.config.js and postcss.config.js without adding any replacement — v4 needs nothing
Replace the content array globs with @source directives but keep everything else identical
questions.answer: Install @tailwindcss/vite, add it to vite.config.ts, replace the three @tailwind directives with @import 'tailwindcss', move theme customisations to @theme {} in CSS, delete tailwind.config.js and postcss.config.js
questions.explanation: The v4 migration has four parts: (1) swap the PostCSS pipeline for @tailwindcss/vite, (2) replace the three @tailwind directives with @import 'tailwindcss', (3) migrate theme customisations from tailwind.config.js into @theme {} blocks in CSS, and (4) delete the now-redundant config and PostCSS files.
